The International Press Centre has urged journalists and media organisations to prioritise citizens’ concerns, scrutinise political promises and hold elected officials accountable ahead of the 2027 elections, rather than focusing primarily on rallies, party defections and campaign activities. The Executive Director of the IPC, Lanre Arogundade, made the call in Abuja during an interface with the Nigeria Union of Journalists on Professional and Democratic Accountability Journalism ahead of the 2027 elections. Arogundade said the media must strengthen its capacity to provide credible, balanced, inclusive and public-interest information as the country approaches another election cycle. He said elections should not be reduced to political campaigns, rallies, candidates and the eventual announcement of results, stressing that citizens’ aspirations, concerns and expectations of leadership must occupy a central position in electoral reporting. According to him, journalists have a responsibility to facilitate informed public discourse, interrogate campaign promises and ensure that the voices of ordinary Nigerians are adequately represented. He said, “This is why we must begin to look beyond event-driven electoral coverage towards more substantive, issue-based, and citizen-centred reporting. “The question before us is not simply how well the media can cover the activities of political parties and candidates. It is also how effectively the media can interrogate campaign promises, document citizens’ priority concerns, verify political claims, monitor the performance of elected officials, and provide the public with the information necessary to assess governance.” The IPC director challenged journalists to examine whether their reports adequately reflected Nigerians’ concerns about the economy, education, healthcare, security, employment and infrastructure. Arogundade warned that sensationalism, unverified claims, inflammatory rhetoric and the unchecked spread of misinformation and disinformation could undermine public confidence, deepen social divisions and weaken democratic institutions. He said, “Conversely, a media environment that prioritises accuracy, fairness, verification, conflict-sensitive reporting, and accountability can strengthen public trust and contribute to peaceful, credible, and inclusive elections.” Tinubu’s frog and the 36 scorpions 2027: Gombe gov urges voters to back Tinubu, APC candidates 2027: PDP inaugurates 22-member committee for Osun senator’s re-election He further urged journalists to strengthen their verification skills and resist pressure to prioritise speed over accuracy, noting that fact-checking must become an integral part of responsible electoral reporting. The IPC executive director also expressed concerns about the safety and professional independence of journalists, insisting that they should be able to discharge their duties without intimidation, harassment or unlawful interference. Similarly, the Chairman of the NUJ, FCT Council, Grace Ike, urged journalists to place citizens at the centre of electoral discourse rather than allow politicians to dictate the direction of election coverage. She said democracy could not thrive where citizens were misinformed, while accountability would remain elusive if the media merely reported events without interrogating promises, policies and performance. Ike said, “As we approach 2027, our reporting must go beyond rallies, defections, press statements and the drama of politics. We must ask the harder questions: “What do citizens truly want? What are their priority concerns on security, the economy, jobs, education, healthcare, infrastructure, and the cost of living? Are candidates offering real solutions, or mere slogans? Are promises being kept, or broken?” She described accountability journalism as putting citizens, rather than politicians, at the centre of electoral conversations. The NUJ chairman identified misinformation, disinformation, hate speech, online manipulation, growing public distrust and safety threats to journalists as challenges confronting the media ahead of the elections. She said verification must take precedence over speed and accuracy over sensationalism, urging journalists to resist being used as instruments of political propaganda. Ike reaffirmed the council’s commitment to professional and ethical journalism, press freedom, fact-checking and the protection of journalists. She added, “Let us give voice to the voiceless — the women, the young people, persons with disabilities, and ordinary Nigerians in communities whose concerns are often ignored until election season.” Deborah Musa Deborah Musa is a journalist at Punch Newspapers with five years of experience in journalism, including three years covering the judiciary.
